newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: No need for minimum wage change - Australia PM.
newsitem.headline: No need for minimum wage change - Australia PM.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard said there was no need to change Australia's minimum wage levels to combat high unemployment, but the community had to understand the impact minimum wage levels had on jobs.

"Whilst I wasn't advocating any change to the Australian (wages) approach I do think if you are to have a sensible debate about this you have to be honest, and you have to say to people why it is that there are differentials," Howard told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.

He had been asked if Australia needed to reasses its relatively high minimum wage and follow the United States system of a low minimum wage which is credited with helping bring down U.S. unemployment.
"One of the reasons why America's unemployment level is lower than Australia is that minimum wages in America are much lower than what they are in Australia," Howard said.
Howard said his Liberal National government would tackle unemployment through better economic growth aand fostering small business.
"We'll get unemployment down through a combination of sustained higher economic growth and greater flexiblity in the labour market," he said.

"In looking at greater flexiblity in the labour market you've got to understand that in a sense countries like America have chosen to have lower minimum wages and through that have purchased lower unemployment."

"Countries like Australia have said that if you get work then ... you ought to be paid, or guaranteed a higher minimum that the United States, that's our ethos, and I think it's a very understandable ethos."
"We have to try and, as it were, secure greater flexibility according to the Australian ethos."
Australia's unemployment rate has been stuck above 8.5 percent since Howard's conservative Liberal-National coalition was elected in March 1996.
Unemployment rose to 8.8 percent in May and economists are expecting the jobless rate to be 8.7 percent in June.
The United State's jobless rate rose to five percent in June after dropping to a near 24-year low of 4.8 percent in May.
